overview.title: Workflow wrap-up; key network architectures
overview.main_topic: The last three steps of the universal workflow (baseline, overfit-then-regularize, deploy and monitor), and an overview of the architecture families with Table 20.1 mapping data modalities to architectures
overview.central_idea: After setup, beat a common-sense baseline, then deliberately overfit and regularize based on validation data only (keeping the test set as a guard against validation overfitting), then deploy and monitor. Architectures encode assumptions about data structure (a hypothesis space); success depends on matching those assumptions to the data, and architectures combine like LEGO bricks.
overview.importance: These are the most practically consequential rules of the book: the order of operations in model development, and how to pick an architecture for a modality. Table 20.1 is a compact lookup table you can reuse on any new problem.
learning_objectives: State the last three workflow steps and the reason for each
Explain why you should first overfit and only then regularize
Explain validation-set overfitting and why a separate test set guards against it
Explain what it means for an architecture to encode assumptions (a hypothesis space)
Use Table 20.1 to pick an architecture for a given input/output modality
prerequisites: Overview of architectures from the book's chapters

summary:
The workflow recap from p.623 concludes with three steps:

5. **Develop a first model that beats a trivial common-sense baseline**, demonstrating that ML can work on your problem, which is not always the case.
6. **Gradually refine the architecture** by tuning hyperparameters and adding regularization, making changes based on **validation data only** (not test or training data). First get the model to **overfit** (finding a capacity greater than needed), and only then add regularization or downsize. Beware of **validation-set overfitting**: hyperparameters can become overspecialized to the validation set; avoiding this is why a separate **test set** exists.
7. **Deploy the final model** (web API, JavaScript or C++ application, embedded device...), **keep monitoring** it on real-world data, and use the findings to refine the next iteration.

Section **20.1.6 Key network architectures** lists the families you should know: **densely connected networks, convolutional networks, recurrent networks, Diffusion Models, and Transformers**. Each targets specific data modalities because an architecture **encodes assumptions about the data's structure**, a **hypothesis space** in which the search for a good model proceeds; whether it works depends entirely on the match between data structure and these assumptions. Architectures combine like **LEGO bricks** into larger multimodal models.

**Table 20.1** maps modalities to models: vector data → densely connected network; timeseries → RNN or Transformer; images → ConvNet; text → Transformer (all four for class probability or regression outputs); text/images → text: Transformer; text/images → images: VAE or Diffusion Model.

The review of each family begins with **densely connected networks**: a stack of `Dense` layers for vector data, where each sample is a vector of numerical or categorical attributes (continued on p.625).

paragraphs.excerpt: Develop a first model that beats a trivial common-sense baseline, thus demonstrating that
paragraphs.what_it_says: Step 5: build a first model that beats a trivial common-sense baseline, showing ML can work on the problem, which may not always be the case.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A baseline is the score of a no-learning strategy: predicting the most frequent class, the mean target, or 'tomorrow equals today' for time series. Beating it shows the model has 'statistical power'; failing to beat it after several reasonable attempts suggests the inputs may not contain the information needed.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Without a baseline, an accuracy of 90% is meaningless (it could be worse than always predicting the majority class).

terminology.meaning: The performance of a trivial, non-learned predictor, used as the minimum bar a model must clear.
The book's term for a model's ability to beat the baseline.

connections: p.205: 6.2.3 Beating a baseline: achieving statistical power.
p.206: 'It's not always possible to achieve statistical power.'

paragraphs.excerpt: Gradually refine your model architecture by tuning hyperparameters and adding regularization. Make changes based
paragraphs.what_it_says: Step 6: refine by tuning hyperparameters and adding regularization, guided by validation performance only. First overfit (to find more capacity than needed), then regularize or downsize. Beware of validation-set overfitting; the separate test set exists to catch it.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The logic: you cannot know the right capacity in advance, so you overshoot (train/val curves diverge), which proves you have enough capacity, then pull back toward the best generalization. Every decision based on validation scores leaks a bit of information about the validation set into the model's design; after many iterations, the configuration may be tuned to validation-set quirks. The test set, never used for decisions, gives an honest final estimate.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Using training data to guide changes rewards memorization; using test data to guide changes destroys your only unbiased estimate.

terminology.meaning: Configuration choices not learned by gradient descent (number of layers, units, learning rate, dropout rate).
Techniques that reduce overfitting (dropout, weight penalties, smaller models, data augmentation).
Hyperparameters becoming overspecialized to the validation set through repeated tuning.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Step 7: deploy (web API, JavaScript or C++ application, embedded device, etc.), keep monitoring performance on real-world data, and use the findings to refine the next iteration.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Deployment is not the end: real-world data drifts away from training data (concept drift), and the only way to notice is monitoring. Monitoring results feed back into problem definition and data collection, closing the loop.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: A model that was accurate at launch can silently degrade; ongoing monitoring and retraining are part of the workflow.

paragraphs.excerpt: The families of network architectures that you should be familiar with after reading this
paragraphs.what_it_says: Key families: densely connected, convolutional, recurrent, Diffusion Models, Transformers. Each fits specific modalities because an architecture encodes assumptions about data structure, a hypothesis space for the search; success depends entirely on matching data structure and architectural assumptions.
paragraphs.what_it_means: An architecture restricts which functions the model can represent. Convolutions assume locality and translation invariance (good for images); recurrent layers assume sequential order with a running state; Transformers assume pairwise token interactions matter (attention) and need positional information for order; Dense layers assume nothing about structure. A good prior shrinks the search space to functions likely to be right, which improves data efficiency.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: When a model fails to generalize despite fitting, a mismatched architecture prior is a prime suspect (p.179).

terminology.meaning: The set of all functions a model with a given architecture can represent; training searches within it.
Assumptions about data structure built into the architecture.

connections: p.28: Machine learning as searching a hypothesis space guided by a feedback signal.
p.179: 'Using better architecture priors' in section 5.3.

paragraphs.excerpt: These different network types can easily be combined to achieve larger multimodal models, much
paragraphs.what_it_says: Network types combine like LEGO bricks into larger multimodal models; deep learning layers are LEGO bricks for information processing. Table 20.1 maps input/output modalities to architectures.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Because every layer maps tensors to tensors and the whole is differentiable, you can plug a ConvNet image encoder and a Transformer text encoder into one model and train end to end. The only constraint is shape compatibility between connected layers.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Real systems (e.g., text-to-image models) are compositions of the families listed here.

terminology.meaning: A model that processes or produces more than one data modality (e.g., text and images).

concepts.name: Common-sense baseline
concepts.definition: The score of a trivial, non-learned predictor that a model must beat.
concepts.intuition: If you cannot beat guessing intelligently, learning is not helping.
concepts.technical: E.g. majority class accuracy; predicting the mean; 'tomorrow = today' for forecasts.
concepts.significance: Step 5 of the workflow; demonstrates statistical power.
concepts.example: On a dataset with 70% negatives, any classifier under 70% accuracy is worse than always predicting negative.
concepts.misconception: That ML always works if you try hard enough; the page notes beating the baseline may not always be possible.

concepts.name: Overfit first, then regularize
concepts.definition: Increase capacity until the model overfits, then add regularization or downsize to maximize validation performance.
concepts.intuition: Find the edge of the cliff before stepping back to the best viewpoint.
concepts.technical: Overfitting shows as diverging training and validation loss; regularization (dropout, weight decay, smaller models) narrows the gap.
concepts.significance: Guarantees you are not limited by insufficient capacity.
concepts.example: Adding layers until validation loss starts rising after a few epochs, then adding dropout.
concepts.misconception: That overfitting should be avoided at all stages; here it is a deliberate diagnostic step.

concepts.name: Validation-set overfitting
concepts.definition: Hyperparameters becoming overspecialized to the validation set through repeated tuning.
concepts.intuition: If you keep re-taking the same practice exam and adjusting, you learn that exam, not the subject.
concepts.technical: Each tuning decision leaks information about validation data into the model; the held-out test set provides an unbiased check.
concepts.significance: The reason a separate test set is needed.
concepts.example: Trying 500 hyperparameter configurations and picking the top validation score.
concepts.misconception: That a model never trained on validation data cannot overfit it.

concepts.name: Architecture as a hypothesis space
concepts.definition: An architecture encodes assumptions about data structure, restricting the space of functions searched during training.
concepts.intuition: Choosing the right-shaped key ring before trying keys.
concepts.technical: Convolution: locality and translation invariance; recurrence: sequential order; attention: pairwise interactions; Dense: no structural assumption.
concepts.significance: 'Whether a given architecture will work on a given problem depends entirely on the match' between data structure and assumptions.
concepts.example: A ConvNet on images vs a Dense network on flattened pixels: the ConvNet is far more data efficient.
concepts.misconception: That a sufficiently big model of any architecture is equally good on any data.

concepts.name: Modality-to-architecture mapping (Table 20.1)
concepts.definition: Default architecture choices per input/output modality.
concepts.intuition: A lookup table for starting new problems.
concepts.technical: Vector→Dense; timeseries→RNN/Transformer; images→ConvNet; text→Transformer; text/images→text: Transformer; text/images→images: VAE/Diffusion.
concepts.significance: Summarizes the book's architecture chapters in six rows.
concepts.misconception: That the mapping is exclusive; e.g. Vision Transformers also process images (p.306).

deeper.title: Why tune only on validation data
deeper.body:
Interpretation of step 6:
- **Training data** decides the weights; using it to judge changes rewards memorization (training loss always drops with more capacity).
- **Validation data** is the feedback signal for design decisions; it slowly leaks into the design.
- **Test data** is touched once at the end; using it for decisions turns it into a second validation set and leaves you with no unbiased estimate.

deeper.title: Priors as data efficiency
deeper.body: Beyond the book: a Dense layer from a 32×32×3 image (3,072 inputs) to 64 units has $3072 \times 64 + 64 = 196{,}672$ parameters and must learn separately that an edge detector at the top-left is useful at the bottom-right. A Conv2D layer with 64 filters of size 3×3 has $3 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 \cdot 64 + 64 = 1{,}792$ parameters and reuses each detector at every location. The convolution's built-in assumption (locality + translation invariance) is exactly the kind of 'assumption about the structure of the data' the page describes.

deeper.title: LEGO bricks for information processing
deeper.body: The book's analogy: bricks of different shapes (layer types) snap together as long as their connectors fit (tensor shapes). A text-to-image system is a build combining a Transformer brick (text encoder) with a diffusion brick (image generator), trained or fine-tuned end to end.

misconceptions.claim: You should add regularization from the start to prevent overfitting.
misconceptions.correction: The book says first get the model to overfit (to confirm sufficient capacity), and only then regularize or downsize.

misconceptions.claim: If the model never trains on the validation set, the validation score is unbiased.
misconceptions.correction: Repeated hyperparameter tuning on it causes validation-set overfitting; the separate test set exists for this reason.
The page says to keep monitoring on real-world data and use findings to refine the next iteration.

misconceptions.claim: The best architecture is independent of the data.
misconceptions.correction: Success depends entirely on matching the data's structure with the architecture's assumptions.

takeaways: Beat a common-sense baseline first; it may turn out that ML cannot solve the problem.
Overfit deliberately, then regularize or downsize, making decisions on validation data only.
Repeated tuning overfits the validation set; the separate test set guards against it.
Deploy, monitor on real-world data, and iterate.
Architectures encode assumptions (a hypothesis space); match them to the data's structure, and combine them like LEGO bricks (Table 20.1).

questions.question: According to the page, which data should guide changes to your model during refinement?
options: A combination of training and test data
questions.explanation: The page says: 'Make changes based on performance on the validation data only, not the test data or the training data.' Training performance rewards memorization, and using the test set for decisions removes your unbiased final estimate.

questions.question: Why should you first get your model to overfit before adding regularization?
questions.answer: Overfitting shows the model has a capacity level greater than needed; once you know capacity is not the bottleneck, you can regularize or downsize to find the best generalization. Starting with regularization risks never reaching sufficient capacity.
questions.explanation: The page states this order explicitly; chapter 6 (p.206-207) develops it.

questions.question: What is validation-set overfitting and what protects you from it?
questions.answer: Hyperparameters becoming overspecialized to the validation set through repeated tuning; a separate test set, used only for final evaluation, protects you.
questions.explanation: Stated at the end of step 6 on the page.

questions.question: According to Table 20.1, which architecture is listed for generating images from text and images?
questions.explanation: The last row of the table maps Text, Images → Images to VAE, Diffusion Model. ConvNet is listed for images → class/regression, RNN/Transformer for timeseries, and Dense networks for vector data.

questions.question: What does the page mean when it says an architecture encodes 'a hypothesis space'? Give an example.
questions.answer: The architecture restricts which functions the model can represent, building in assumptions about the data's structure; training then searches only within that space. Example: convolutions assume local patterns that are useful at any position (translation invariance), which suits images.
questions.explanation: Whether a model works depends on the match between those assumptions and the data's actual structure.

questions.question: Name three deployment targets mentioned in step 7 and what you should keep doing after deployment.
questions.answer: A web API, a JavaScript or C++ application, an embedded device; keep monitoring performance on real-world data and use the findings to refine the next iteration.
